text:
NLP
• Goal of NLP: get computers to perform useful tasks
involving human language, e.g.:
 enabling human-machine communication
 improving human-human communication
 doing useful processing of text or speech, etc.
• Conversational agents (e.g. HAL 9000 computer in
Stanley Kubrick’s film 2001: A Space Odyssey;
Apple SIRI, Amazon Alexa, …)
 Analyse language input (Automatic Speech
Recognition and N.L. Understanding)
 Analyse language output (NL generation and Speech
Synthesis).
• Machine Translation
4

text:
NLP (cont.)
• Web-based Question Answering
 Definition questions
 Factoid questions.
 More complex questions (How, Why):
 information embedded in other text on a Web page,
 doing inference (drawing conclusions based on known facts),
 synthesizing and summarizing information from multiple
sources or web pages.
• Modern understanding systems, including Info.
Extraction, Word Sense Disambiguation
• This chapter summarizes the kinds of knowledge
necessary for these tasks (and others like spell
correction, grammar checking, …) and (throughout
the course) the needed mathematical models. 5

text:
Is NLP Important?
• A huge amount of knowledge now available
electronically in the form of NL texts (online
journals, Wikipedia, etc.)
 In 2025, global data creation projected to grow to
about 180 zettabytes (1021 Bytes)
• Conversational agents now an important form of
human-machine communication and work: think
of chatbots, generative AI
• Much human-human communication is facilitated
by machines: e.g. MT and Speech-to-speech
MT, text summarisation, etc.
7

text:
“Breaking Down The Numbers: How
Much Data Does The World Create
Daily in 2024?” (Edge Delta)
• Facebook produces ~ 4,000 TB daily, ranking
#1 in “most visited sites globally in 2023”.
• X (Twitter) garners around 500 million tweets
daily, which amounts to 560 GB of data.
• Google processes around 3.5 billion searches
daily, amounting to 20 PB.
• In 2023, the average internet user created
about 1.7 MB of data per second, i.e. 146.88
GB daily.

text:
18
NLP, a key Solution to the datasphere
size and multilingualism !
 Branch of AI at the crossroads of Linguistics, CS,
Mathematics, & Statistics.
 Aim: to develop IT tools that can understand and
generate natural language so as to make the use of
technology seamless / intuitive / natural:
 Answer semantically richer questions by getting
information from the Web
 Get help/advice through conversations with the computer
/ smart phone (virtual assistants, conversational agents)
 Automatically generate text summaries
 Translate documents into different languages
 Etc.

text:
• الثورة الجزائرية ضد الاستعمار الفرنسي بدأت في1 نوفمبر1954 ، وكانت نتيجة لعدة عوامل تاريخية
وسياسية واقتصادية. إليك بعض النقاط الرئيسية حول كيفية قيام الشعب الجزائري بالثورة:
•الأسباب التاريخية: عانت الجزائر من الاستعمار الفرنسي منذ عام 1830 ، حيث تم استغلال الموارد
والثروات، وتم تطبيق سياسات تمييزية ضد الجزائريين.
•الوعي الوطني: في بداية القرن العشرين، بدأ الوعي الوطني يزداد بين الجزائريين. نشأت حركات
سياسية وثقافية تدعو إلى الاستقلال والحقوق المدنية.
•العدوان والظلم: تزايدت الأعمال القمعية ضد الشعب الجزائري، مما أدى إلى استياء واسع النطاق.
العديد من الجزائريين كانوا يعيشون في ظروف اقتصادية صعبة وحرمان من الحقوق.
•التنظيم: في عام 1954 ، تأسست جبهة التحرير الوطني(FLN)  كحركة سياسية وعسكرية تهدف إلى
تحقيق الاستقلال. كانت الجبهة منظمة بشكل جيد ولديها دعم شعبي.
•اندلاع الثورة: في ليلة 1 نوفمبر1954 ، شن مقاتلو جبهة التحرير الوطني هجمات منسقة على مراكز
الشرطة والمكاتب الحكومية، مما أطلق شرارة الثورة.
•الدعم الدولي: حظيت الثورة بدعم من العديد من الدول والشعوب الأخرى، وأصبحت قضية الجزائر
موضوع اهتمام دولي.
•الحرب الطويلة: استمرت الثورة حتى عام 1962 ، وشهدت مواجهات عسكرية شرسة، مع استخدام
الطرف الفرنسي لأساليب قمعية، لكن الجبهة نجحت في الحفاظ على مقاومة مستمرة.
•الاستقلال: في عام 1962، تم التوصل إلى اتفاق إيفيان، الذي أدى إلى إعلان استقلال الجزائر في 5
يوليو من نفس العام.
•تُعتبر الثورة الجزائرية واحدة من أبرز الحركات التحررية في القرن العشرين، وقد تركتأثراً عميقاً
على الهوية الوطنية الجزائرية. 30

text:
NLP Applications?
• Counting words (wc)?
 When one counts words: Yes
 To count words, you need to know what a word is
 knowledge of the language.
• NB: wc on Unix compiled for English will not work
for Chinese!
 When it counts lines and bytes: No
 Lines and bytes are programming artifacts, not
linguistic entities.
• This is still very simplistic. Developing
Conversational Agents (e.g. HAL) requires
much deeper/richer modeling of a language!

text:
Types of Knowledge of Language
• Phonetics and Phonology: knowledge about
linguistic sounds.
• Morphology: knowledge of the meaningful
components of words.
• Syntax: knowledge of the structural relationships
between words.
• (Lexical & compositional) Semantics : knowledge
of meaning.
• Pragmatics: knowledge of the relationship of
meaning to the goals and intentions of the speaker.
• Discourse: knowledge about linguistic units larger
than a single utterance. E.g. How many states were in
the US that year? (case of coreference resolution)

Models

Words, Word Embeddings, …)

• In Python regular expressions use backslash "\" for
special characters. You must type extra backslashes!

not a "slash" followed by an "n". Need "\\n" for
the two characters.
• Instead: use Python's raw string notation for
regex:
 r"[tT]he"
 r"\d+" matches one or more digits
• instead of "\\d+"

text:
Lookahead assertions
• (?= pattern) is true if pattern matches, but is zero-
width; doesn't advance character pointer
• (?! pattern) true if a pattern does not match
• How to match, at the beginning of a line, any single word
that doesn’t start with “Volcano”:
/ˆ(?!Volcano)[A-Za-z]+/
• In Python:
# Pattern to match "First" at the beginning of a
line
pattern = r'^First'
# Using re.MULTILINE to allow ^ to match the start
# of each line (e.g. text string on several lines)
matches = re.findall(pattern, text, re.MULTILINE) 22

(Kudo, 2018)

 A token segmenter that takes a raw test sentence

text:

token learner
Let a vocabulary be the set of all individual
characters

Dynamic Programming for
Minimum Edit Distance
• Dynamic programming: A tabular
computation of D(n,m)
• Solving problems by combining solutions to
subproblems.
• Bottom-up
 We compute D(i,j) for small i,j
 And compute larger D(i,j) based on previously
computed smaller values
 i.e., compute D(i,j) for all i (0 < i < n)  and
j (0 < j < m)

(Levenshtein)
• Initialization
D(i,0) = i
D(0,j) = j
• Recurrence Relation:
For each  i = 1…M
For each  j = 1…N
D(i-1,j) + 1
D(i,j)= min D(i,j-1) + 1
D(i-1,j-1)+ 2; if X(i) ≠ Y(j)
0; if X(i) = Y(j)
• Termination:
D(N,M) is the distance

Where did the name, dynamic
programming, come from?
…The 1950s were not good years for mathematical research.
[the] Secretary of Defense …had a pathological fear and hatred of
the word, research…
I decided therefore to use the word, “programming”.
I wanted to get across the idea that this was dynamic, this was
multistage… I thought, let’s … take a word that has an absolutely
precise meaning, namely dynamic… it’s impossible to use the
word, dynamic, in a pejorative sense. Try thinking of some
combination that will possibly give it a pejorative meaning. It’s
impossible.
Thus, I thought dynamic programming was a good name. It was
something not even a Congressman could object to.”
Richard Bellman, “Eye of the Hurricane: an autobiography” 1984.

• Recall the definition of conditional probabilities
p(B|A) = P(A,B)/P(A)

• The Chain Rule in General
P(x1,x2,x3,…,xn) =
P(x1)P(x2|x1)P(x3|x1,x2)…P(xn|x1,…,x`)

text:
Intrinsic (in-vitro) evaluation
• Extrinsic evaluation not always possible
• Expensive, time-consuming
• Intrinsic evaluation metric: one that measures
the quality of a model independent of any
application.
• Perplexity: standard intrinsic metric for
measuring LM performance:
• Directly measures LM performance at predicting
words.
• Doesn't necessarily correspond with real application
performance
• Gives us a single general metric for LMs
• Useful for large language models (LLMs) as well as
n-grams

Training on the test set
• We can’t allow test sentences into the
training set.
• Or else the LM will assign that sentence an
artificially high probability when we see it in
the test set.
• And hence assign the whole test set a falsely
high probability.

• This is called “Training on the test set”

text:
• Use perplexity instead of raw probability
• Probability depends on the size of the test set
• Probability gets smaller the longer the text
• Better to have a metric that is per-word, normalized by length so we can compare across texts of different lengths.
• Perplexity is the inverse probability of the test set, normalized by the number of words $N$:

$$PP(W) = P(w_1, w_2, \dots, w_N)^{-\frac{1}{N}} = \sqrt[N]{\frac{1}{P(w_1, w_2, \dots, w_N)}}$$

Using the chain rule:
$$PP(W) = \left[ \prod_{i=1}^N P(w_i \mid w_1, \dots, w_{i-1}) \right]^{-\frac{1}{N}}$$

36

text:
• Perplexity is one of the most important metrics in NLP, used for evaluating large language models as well as n-gram models.
• Perplexity is the inverse probability of the test set, normalized by the number of words (or tokens).
• Probability range is $[0, 1]$, perplexity range is $[1, \infty]$.
• The higher the probability of the word sequence, the lower the perplexity. Minimizing perplexity amounts to maximizing the test set probability:

$$\ln PP(W) = -\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \ln P(w_i \mid w_{<i}) = \mathcal{L}_{CE} \implies PP(W) = e^{\mathcal{L}_{CE}}$$

37

text:
Intuition of perplexity:
Weighted average branching factor
• Perplexity is also the weighted average branching factor of a
language.
• Branching factor: number of possible next words that can follow any
word
Example: Deterministic language L = {red, blue, green}
Branching factor = 3 (any word can be followed by red, blue, green)
Now assume LM A where each word follows any other word with equal
probability ⅓
Given a test set T = "red red red red blue"
PerplexityA(T) = PA(red red red red blue)= ((⅓)5)-1/5 = (⅓)-1 = 3
• But now suppose red was very likely in training set, such that for LM B:
 P(red) = .8   p(green) = .1  p(blue) = .1
• We would expect the probability to be higher, and hence the perplexity to
be smaller:
PerplexityB(T) = PB(red red red red blue)-1/5 = (.8 * .8 * .8 * .8 * .1) -1/5
=.04096 -1/5  =.527-1 = 1.89 39

text:
The Perils of Overfitting
• Problem with using maximum likelihood
estimates for probabilities: any finite training
corpus will be missing some perfectly
acceptable English word sequences.
• N-grams only work well for word prediction if the test
corpus looks like the training corpus
• But even when we try to pick a good training
corpus, the test set will surprise us!
• We need to train robust models that generalize!
• One kind of generalization: Zeros
• Things that don’t ever occur in the training set
• But occur in the test set
53

text:
Maximum Likelihood Estimates
• The maximum likelihood estimate
 of some parameter of a model M from a training set T
 maximizes the likelihood of the training set T given the
model M
• Suppose the word “bagel” occurs 400 times in a
corpus of a million words
• What is the probability that a random word from
some other text will be “bagel”?
• MLE estimate is 400/1,000,000 = .0004
• This may be a bad estimate for some other corpus
 But it is the estimate that makes it most likely that
“bagel” will occur 400 times in a million word corpus.

text:
EM Algorithm
• With n-gram models, the typical approach involves the following:
1. With the Training Set: Compute N-gram Models (Model building): You
compute the unigram, bigram, and trigram probabilities based on the training set.
This involves counting the occurrences of each n-gram and calculating the
corresponding probabilities.
2. With the Held-out Set: EM Steps: EM algorithm applied to this set to optimize
the parameters (mixture weights) for the model.
 Initialize Parameters: Set initial mixture weights for combining the models.
 E-step: Using the held-out set, calculate the expected contributions from each
n-gram model to the observed data.
 M-step: Update the mixture weights based on these expected contributions.
 Iterate: Repeat the E-step and M-step until convergence, using the held-out
set for evaluation.
• With a held-out Set:
 Avoid Overfitting.
 Model performance evaluation after each iteration of the EM algorithm,
ensuring that the adjustments made lead to improved performance on unseen
data.
70

text:
The EM Algorithm
Model Overview
• Unigram: Probability of w3 based solely on its
frequency in the corpus, P(w3).
• Bigram: Probability of w3 given w2, P(w3​∣w2).
• Trigram: Probability of w3 given w1 and w2,
P(w3​∣w1,w2).
• overall probability of w3 can be expressed as:
P(w3∣w1,w2)=λ1 P(w3) +  λ2 P(w3​∣w2) +  λ3 P(w3​∣w1,w2)
where λ1,λ2,λ3 are the weights (mixture coefficients)
that determine the contribution of each model.
Step 1: Initialize Parameters
• Initial Weights: Set initial values for λ1,λ2,λ3. As
equal or based on some heuristic (e.g., prior
knowledge about the importance of the n-grams)
λ1+λ2+λ3=1.
• Model Parameters: Also initialize the counts needed
for unigram, bigram, and trigram probabilities from
the training corpus. 71

Model Overview
• Unigram: Probability of w3 based solely on its

• Bigram: Probability of w3 given w2, P(w3​∣w2).
• Trigram: Probability of w3 given w1 and w2,
P(w3​∣w1,w2).
• overall probability of w3 can be expressed as:
P(w3∣w1,w2)=λ1 P(w3) +  λ2 P(w3​∣w2) +  λ3 P(w3​∣w1,w2)
where λ1,λ2,λ3 are the weights (mixture coefficients)
that determine the contribution of each model.
Step 1: Initialize Parameters
• Initial Weights: Set initial values for λ1,λ2,λ3. As
equal or based on some heuristic (e.g., prior
knowledge about the importance of the n-grams)
λ1+λ2+λ3=1.
• Model Parameters: Also initialize the counts needed
for unigram, bigram, and trigram probabilities from
the training corpus. 71

text:
The EM Algorithm (cont.)
• Step 2: E-Step (Expectation Step)
Calculate the expected counts for each word
based on the current estimates of λ1, λ2, and
λ3.
Expected Counts for Trigram: For a
trigram(w1,w2,w3):
E[C(w3∣w1,w2)] = λ3 P(w3∣w1,w2)⋅count(w1,w2)
Expected Counts for Bigram: For a bigram
(w2,w3): E[C(w3∣w2)] = λ2 P(w3∣w2)⋅count(w2)
Expected Counts for Unigram: For a unigram
w3:
E[C(w3)] = λ1 P(w3)⋅N
(where N is the total number of words)
72

The EM Algorithm (cont.)
• Step 2: E-Step (Expectation Step)
Calculate the expected counts for each word
based on the current estimates of λ1, λ2, and
λ3.
Expected Counts for Trigram: For a
trigram(w1,w2,w3):
E[C(w3∣w1,w2)] = λ3 P(w3∣w1,w2)⋅count(w1,w2)
Expected Counts for Bigram: For a bigram
(w2,w3): E[C(w3∣w2)] = λ2 P(w3∣w2)⋅count(w2)
Expected Counts for Unigram: For a unigram
w3:
E[C(w3)] = λ1 P(w3)⋅N
(where N is the total number of words)
72

text:
The EM Algorithm (cont.)
• Step 3: M-Step (Maximization Step)
Update the mixing weights based on the expected
counts calculated in the E-step.
Calculate Total Counts: For each w3:
TotalCount(w3) = E[C(w3)]+E[C(w3∣w2)]+E[C(w3∣w1,w2)]
Update the λ Values: The new mixing weights are
calculated as:
λ1′ = ∑w3 E[C(w3)] / ∑w3Total Count(w3)
λ2′ = ∑w3 E[C(w3∣w2)] / ∑w3 Total Count(w3)
λ3′=∑w3E[C(w3∣w1,w2)]∑w3Total Count(w3)
Normalization: Ensure that λ1′+λ2′+λ3′= 1
Step 4: Iterate: Repeat the E-step and M-step
until convergence (i.e., until the changes in
λ1, λ2, and λ3 are negligible).
73

text:
Unknown words: Open versus
closed vocabulary tasks
• If we know all the words in advance
 Vocabulary V is fixed
 Closed vocabulary task
• Often we don’t know this
 Out Of Vocabulary = OOV words
 Open vocabulary task
• Instead: create an unknown word token <UNK>
 Training of <UNK> probabilities
 Create a fixed lexicon L of size V
 At text normalization phase, any training word not in L changed
to  <UNK>
 Now we train its probabilities like a normal word
 At decoding time
 If text input: Use UNK probabilities for any word not in training
74

Stop words
• Some systems ignore stop words

 Call the top 10 or 50 most frequent words the stopword
list.

if they were never there!
• But removing stop words doesn't usually help
• So in practice most NB algorithms use all words and
don't use stopword lists

text:
Optimizing for sentiment analysis
• Standard naive Bayes text classification can work
well for SA, but some small changes are generally
employed that improve performance
• For tasks like SA, word occurrence seems to be
more important than word frequency.
 The occurrence of the word fantastic tells us a lot
 The fact that it occurs 5 times may not tell us much more.
• This variant is called Binary multinomial Naive
Bayes, or just Binary NB:
 Clip the word counts at 1
 Same algorithm as before except that
 For each document remove all duplicate words before
concatenating them into the single big document during
training and
 Remove duplicate words from test documents.

text:
Sentiment Classification: Handling Negation
Simple baseline method:
• Add NOT_ to every word after a token of logical negation (n’t, not,
no, never) until the next punctuation mark:
didn’t like this movie, but I
didn’t NOT_like NOT_this NOT_movie, but I
• Newly formed ‘words’ like NOT like, NOT recommend will thus occur
more often in negative documents and act as cues for negative
sentiment,
• Words like NOT bored, NOT dismiss will acquire positive
associations.
• Syntactic parsing (Chapter 18) can be used to handle the details of
the grammatical relationships
• This simple baseline works quite well in practice.
44

text:
Using Lexicons in Sentiment Classification
• Add a feature that gets a count whenever a word from
the lexicon occurs
 E.g., a feature called "this word occurs in the positive
lexicon" or "this word occurs in the negative lexicon"
• Now all positive words (good, great, beautiful, wonderful)
or negative words count for that feature.
• Worked out scenario.
• Using 1-2 features isn't as good as using all the words.
• But when training data is sparse or not representative of
the test set, dense lexicon features can help
• Using just two features (positive and negative counts),
the model is simplified while still capturing important
sentiment information.
•  This can help improve performance, especially in cases
where individual words might not provide enough data
due to sparsity.
48

• Add a feature that gets a count whenever a word from
the lexicon occurs
 E.g., a feature called "this word occurs in the positive
lexicon" or "this word occurs in the negative lexicon"
• Now all positive words (good, great, beautiful, wonderful)
or negative words count for that feature.
• Worked out scenario.
• Using 1-2 features isn't as good as using all the words.
• But when training data is sparse or not representative of
the test set, dense lexicon features can help
• Using just two features (positive and negative counts),
the model is simplified while still capturing important
sentiment information.
•  This can help improve performance, especially in cases
where individual words might not provide enough data
due to sparsity.
48

text:
Naive Bayes in Language ID
• Determining what language a piece of text is written in:
 Features based on character n-grams do very well
 E.g. 2-grams (‘zw’) 3-grams (‘nya’, ‘ Vo’), or 4-grams
(‘ie z’, ‘thei’), or, even simpler byte n-grams
• Language ID systems are trained on multilingual text,
such as Wikipedia (Wikipedia text in 68 different
languages was used in (Lui and Baldwin, 2011)), or
newswire
• Important to train on lots of varieties of each language
(e.g., American English varieties like African-American
English, or English varieties around the world like
Indian English)

text:
Representational Harms
• Harms caused by a system that demeans a social group
• Such as by perpetuating negative stereotypes about them.
• Kiritchenko and Mohammad 2018 study
• Examined 200 sentiment analysis systems on pairs of sentences
• Identical except for names:
• common African American (Shaniqua) or European American
(Stephanie).
• Like "I talked to Shaniqua yesterday" vs "I talked to Stephanie
yesterday"
• Result: systems assigned lower sentiment and more negative
emotion to sentences with African American names
• Downstream harm:
• Perpetuates stereotypes about African Americans
• African Americans treated differently by NLP tools like sentiment
A. (widely used in marketing research, mental health studies, etc.)
69

text:
Harms of Censorship
• Toxicity detection: text classification task of detecting hate
speech, abuse, harassment, or other kinds of toxic language.
• Widely used in online content moderation
• Toxicity classifiers incorrectly flag non-toxic sentences that simply
mention minority identities (like the words "blind")
• women (Park et al., 2018),
• disabled people (Hutchinson et al., 2020)
• Downstream harms:
• Censorship of speech by disabled people and other groups
• Speech by these groups becomes less visible online
• Writers might be nudged by these algorithms to avoid these
words making people less likely to write about themselves or
these groups.
• Any positive facet of this?
70

for writers who are African American (Blodgett
and O'Connor 2017) or from India (Jurgens et

text:
Harms in Text Classification
• Causes:
• Issues in the data; NLP systems amplify biases in training
data
• Problems in the labels
• Problems in the algorithms (like what the model is
trained to optimize)
• Prevalence: The same problems occur throughout
NLP (including large language models)
• Solutions?: There are no general mitigations or
solutions
• But harm mitigation is an active area of research
• And there are standard benchmarks and tools that we
can use for measuring some of the harms

Components of a probabilistic machine
learning classifier
1. A feature representation of the input.
For each input observation x(i), a vector of features [x1, x2, ... , xn].
Feature i for input x(j) is xi, more completely  xi(j), or sometimes fi  (x).
2. A classification function that computes ො𝑦, the estimated
class, via p(y|x), like the sigmoid or softmax functions.
3. An objective function for learning, like cross-entropy
loss.
4. An algorithm for optimizing the objective function:
stochastic gradient descent.

text:
The two phases of Logistic Regression
• Training: we learn weights w and b using
stochastic gradient descent and cross-entropy
loss.
• Test: Given a test example x, we compute
p(y|x) using learned weights w and b, and
return whichever label (y = 1 or y = 0) has
higher probability.

text:
Binary Classification in Logistic Regression
• Goal of binary LR: train a classifier that can make
a binary decision about the class of a new input
observation
• Given a series of input/output pairs: (x(i), y(i))
• For each observation x(i)
 We represent x(i) by a feature vector [x1, x2,…, xn]
 We compute an output: a predicted class ෢𝑦 𝑖  {0,1}

text:
Logistic Regression for one observation
• Input observation: vector  x = [x1, x2,…, xn]
• Weights: one per feature: W = [w1, w2,…, wn]
 Sometimes the weights are called  θ = [θ1, θ2,…, θn]
• Output: a predicted class y  {0,1}^
(For multinomial logistic regression: y  {0, 1, 2, 3, 4})
• The output is considered as a linear function of
the output
17

text:
How to get the W’s?
• Supervised classification: we know the
correct label y (either 0 or 1) for each x.
• What the system produces is an estimate, ො𝑦
• We want to set w and b to minimize the
distance between our estimate ො𝑦(i) and the
true y (i).
• We need a distance estimator: a loss
function or a cost function
• We need an optimization algorithm to
update w and b to minimize the loss.

text:
Mini-batch training
• Stochastic gradient descent chooses a single
random example at a time.
• That can result in choppy movements
• More common to compute gradient over batches of
training instances.
• Batch training: entire dataset
• Mini-batch training: m examples at a time (512,
or 1024)
• Mini-batches can easily be vectorized
• Size of the minibatch based on the computational
resources.
 Can process all the examples in one mini-batch in
parallel and then accumulate the loss
- not possible with individual or batch training.
61

Overfitting
• A model that perfectly matches the training
data has a problem.

noise

happens to only occur in one class) will get a very
high weight.
 Failing to generalize to a test set without this
word.
• A good model should be able to generalize
well to the unseen (test) data
• A model that overfits will have poor
generalization

the model doesn't generalize well to the test set

text:
L1 vs L2 Regularization
• Both are commonly used in language processing.
• L2 regularization: easier to optimize because of its
simple derivative (the derivative of 𝜃2 is just 2𝜃)
• L1 regularization: more complex (the derivative of
|𝜃| is non-continuous at zero).
• L2 prefers weight vectors with many small weights
• L1 prefers sparse solutions with some larger
weights but many more weights set to zero.
 L1 regularization leads to much sparser weight
vectors, i.e. far fewer features.
69

text:
Intuition: why vectors?
• Consider sentiment analysis:
 With words,  a feature is a word identity
 Feature 5: 'The previous word was "terrible"'
 Requires exact same word to be in the training
and test sets
 With embeddings:
 Feature is a word vector
 'The previous word was vector [35,22,17…]
 Now in the test set we might see a similar vector
[34,21,14]
 We can generalize to similar but unseen words!!!

• Given two documents, we can compute their document
vectors d1 and d2, and estimate the similarity between
the two documents by cos(d1,d2).

paraphrases, tracking changes in word meaning, etc.

text:
Sparse versus dense vectors
• Why dense vectors?
 Short vectors may be easier to use as features in
machine learning (fewer weights to tune)
 Dense vectors may generalize better
 Dense vectors may do better at capturing
synonymy:
 In a sparse vector representation, dimensions for car
and automobile (synonyms) are distinct and
unrelated
• a word with car as a neighbor and a word with
automobile as a neighbor should be similar, but aren't
 In practice, dense vectors work better 68

text:
Word2vec
• Instead of counting how often each word w occurs
near "apricot"
 Train a classifier on a binary prediction task:
 Is w likely to show up near "apricot"?
• We don’t actually care about this task
 But we'll take the learned classifier weights as
the word embeddings
• The big idea is  self-supervision:
 A word c that occurs near apricot in the corpus acts
as the gold "correct answer" for supervised learning
 No need for human labels
(Bengio et al. (2003); Collobert et al. (2011) )

text:
Dot product to compute Similarity
• Intuition of the Skip-gram model:
 base this probability on embedding similarity; i.e.
 a word is likely to occur near the target if its embedding
vector is similar to the target embedding.
• Recall that: two vectors are similar if they have a high
dot product
 Cosine is just a normalized dot product
• So:
 Similarity(w, c) ≈ w ∙ c
• Note: We’ll need to normalize to get a probability
 (cosine isn't a probability either)

• Initial State: Initialize the parameters (weights) of
the model. The matrices W and C represent these
parameters in the context of Word2Vec.

word.

word.
• Learning from Data: As one goes through the
training corpus, the Skip-gram model learns which
word pairs (target, context) co-occur frequently and
adjusts the embeddings in W and C to reflect the
relationships between words.

text:
Two sets of embeddings
• Skip-gram with negative sampling (SGNS) learns two
sets of embeddings
 Target embeddings matrix W
 Context embeddings matrix C
• It is common to just add them up, representing
word i as the vector  wi + ci
• Alternatively, one can throw away the C matrix and
just represent each word i by the vector wi.
• The context window size L affects the performance
of skip-gram embeddings; experiments often tune
the parameter L on a devset.

text:
Summary: How to learn word2vec
(skip-gram) embeddings
• Start with V random d-dimensional vectors as initial
embeddings
• Train a classifier based on embedding similarity
 Take a corpus and take pairs of words that co-occur as
positive examples
 Take as negative examples pairs of words that don't co-
occur
 Train the classifier to distinguish these by slowly
adjusting all the embeddings to improve the classifier
performance
 Throw away the classifier code and keep the
embeddings. 93

Caveats with the parallelogram method
• It only seems to work for frequent words,
small distances and certain relations (relating
countries to capitals, or Parts-of-Speech), but
not others. (Linzen 2016; Gladkova et al. 2016;
Ethayarajh et al. 2019a)
• Understanding analogy is an open area of
research (Peterson et al. 2020)

text:
Embeddings reflect cultural bias!
• Ask “Paris : France :: Tokyo : x”
 x = Japan
• Ask “father : doctor :: mother : x”
 x = nurse
• Ask “man : computer programmer :: woman : x”
 x = homemaker
Bolukbasi, Tolga, Kai-Wei Chang, James Y. Zou, Venkatesh Saligrama, and Adam T. Kalai. "Man is to computer
programmer as woman is to homemaker? debiasing word embeddings." In NeurIPS, pp. 4349-4357. 2016.
• Algorithms that use embeddings as part of e.g.,
hiring searches for programmers, might lead to
bias in hiring 101

text:
Historical embedding as a tool to study
cultural biases
• Compute a gender or ethnic bias for each adjective:
e.g., how much closer the adjective is to "woman"
synonyms than "man" synonyms, or names of particular
ethnicities.
• Embeddings for competence adjective (smart, wise,
brilliant, resourceful, thoughtful, logical) are biased
toward men, a bias slowly decreasing 1960-1990
• Embeddings for dehumanizing adjectives (barbaric,
monstrous, bizarre)  were biased toward Asians in the
1930s, bias decreasing over the 20th century.
• These match the results of old surveys done in the 1930s
Garg, N., Schiebinger, L., Jurafsky, D., and Zou, J. (2018). Word embeddings quantify 100 years of gender
and ethnic stereotypes. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 115(16), E3635–E3644.
102

text:
Why?
• Perceptrons are linear classifiers
• Perceptron equation given x1 and x2, is the
equation of a line
w1x1 + w2x2 + b = 0
• (in standard linear format: x2 = (−w1/w2)x1 + (−b/w2))
• This line acts as a decision boundary
0 if input is on one side of the line
1 if on the other side of the line

classifying an entire test set of examples
• Use matrix multiplication to do the computation

text:
N-gram models vs. neural LMs
• Neural LMs can
 handle much longer histories,
 can generalize better over contexts of similar
words, and
 are more accurate at word-prediction.
• But neural net LMs are
 much more complex,
 slower and need more energy to train, and
 less interpretable than n-gram models.
• So for some smaller tasks n-gram LMs are
still the right tool.

text:
Simple FF Neural Language Models
• Task: At each timestep t predict proba. of next
word wt given prior words wt-1, wt-2, wt-3, …
• Problem: We are now dealing with sequences of
arbitrary length.
• Solution: Use sliding windows (of fixed length)
• i.e. the FF neural LM approximates the probability
of a word given the entire prior context P(wt |w1:t-1)
by approximating based on the N – 1 previous
words.
52

Simple FF Neural LMs (NLMs)
• Example: we will use a 4-gram case, so
we’ll show a neural net to estimate the
probability P(wt = i| wt-3, wt-2, wt-1).
• NLMs represent words in this prior context
by their embeddings, rather than just by
their word identity as used in n-gram LMs.
• This allows them to generalize better to
unseen data.

Why Neural LMs work better than
N-gram LMs
• Suppose:
• Training data:
 We've seen:
I have to make sure that the cat gets fed.
 Never seen:   dog gets fed
• Test data:
 I forgot to make sure that the dog gets ___
 N-gram LMs can't predict "fed"!
 Neural LMs can use similarity of "cat" and "dog"
embeddings to generalize and predict “fed” after
dog

• Forward inference: given an input, run a
forward pass on the network to produce a
probability distribution over possible outputs, in
this case next words.
1. Represent each of the N previous words as a
one-hot vector of length |V|.
2. Multiply these one-hot vectors by the
embedding matrix E.
 E has a column for each word, each being a
column vector of d dimensions
 E has dimensionality d x |V|

• For every training tuple (𝑥, 𝑦)
 Run forward computation to find our estimate ො𝑦
 Run backward computation to update weights:
 For every output node
 Compute loss 𝐿 between true 𝑦 and the estimated ො𝑦
 For every weight 𝑤 from hidden layer to the output
layer
 Update the weight
 For every hidden node
 Assess how much blame it deserves for the current
answer
 For every weight 𝑤 from input layer to the hidden layer
 Update the weight

text:
Why Computation Graphs
• For training, we need the derivative of the
loss with respect to each weight in every
layer of the network
• But the loss is computed only at the very
end of the network!
• Solution: error backpropagation (Rumelhart,
Hinton, Williams, 1986)
• Backprop is a special case of backward
differentiation
• Which relies on computation graphs.

Summary
• For training, we need the derivative of the
loss with respect to weights in early layers of
the network
• But loss is computed only at the very end of
the network!
• Solution: backward differentiation
(Backpropagation)
• Given a computation graph and the
derivatives of all the functions in, it we can
automatically compute the derivative of the
loss with respect to these early weights.

text:
Recurrent Neural Networks
• Language is an inherently temporal phenomenon.
Language is a sequence of events over time.
• This temporal nature is reflected in some language processing

RNNs as Language Models
A FF NLM An RNN language model
moving through a text
• The n-gram language models compute the probability of a word given
counts of its occurrence with the n-1 prior words. (Context size is n-1.)
• For the FF LMs, the context size is the window size.
• RNNs thus don’t have the limited context problem, since the hidden
state can represent information about all of the preceding words.
• RNN LMs process the input sequence one word at a time,
attempting to predict the next word from the current word and the
previous hidden state.

text:
Forward Inference
• Forward inference is the task, given an input, of running a
forward pass on the network to produce a probability distribution
over possible outputs (next words).
• The input sequence X=[x1,…,xN] consists of a series of words
each represented as a one-hot vector of size |V|1,
• The output prediction, y, is a vector representing a probability
distribution over the vocabulary.
• At each step, the model uses the word embedding matrix E to
retrieve the embedding for the current word, and then combines it
with the hidden layer from the previous step to compute a new
hidden layer.
• This hidden layer is then used to generate an output layer which is
passed through a softmax layer to generate a probability
distribution over the entire vocabulary.
13

text:
Training an RNN LM
• self-supervision: To train an RNN as a language model, we take
a corpus of text as training material and at each time step t ask the
model to predict the next word.
• We train the model to minimize the error in predicting the
true next word in the training sequence, using cross-entropy
as the loss function.
– Recall that the cross-entropy loss measures the difference
between a predicted probability distribution and the correct
distribution.
– The correct distribution yt comes from knowing the next word.
– At time t the CE loss is the negative log probability the model
assigns to the next word in the training sequence.
16

text:
Training an RNN language model
• At each word position t, the model takes the correct sequence of tokens w1:t , and
computes a probability distribution over possible next words to compute the model’s
loss for next token wt+1.
– Then we ignore what the model predicted for the next word and instead use the
correct sequence of tokens w1:t+1 to estimate the probability of token wt+2.
– The idea that the model use the correct history sequence to predict the next word
(rather than feeding the model its best case from the previous time step) is called
teacher forcing.
The weights in the
network are adjusted
to minimize the
average CE loss over
the training
sequence via
gradient descent.
17

Stacked RNNs
• Recurrent networks are quite flexible.
– The entire sequence of outputs from one RNN as an input sequence to another one.

• The output of a lower level

last network serving as the final
output.

outperform single-layer
networks.
• As the number of stacks is
increased the training costs rise
quickly.

abstractions for further layers—representations that might prove difficult to induce
in a single RNN.

Bidirectional RNNs
• The RNN uses information from the left context to make its predictions at time t.
• But many NLP applications may require right context in addition to left context.
• A bidirectional RNN combines two independent RNNs, one where the input is
processed from the start to the end, and the other from the end to the start.
– We then concatenate the two representations computed by the networks into a single vector
that captures both the left and right contexts of an input at each point in time.
A bidirectional RNN
• Separate models are trained in
the forward and backward
directions, with the output of
each model at each time point
concatenatedto represent the
bidirectional stateat that time
point.

ℎ𝑡𝑏= 𝑅𝑁𝑁𝑏𝑎𝑐𝑘𝑤𝑎𝑟𝑑(𝑥𝑡, … , 𝑥𝑛)
ℎ𝑡 = [ℎ𝑡𝑓; ℎ𝑡𝑏] # concatenates the outputs of the forward and backward pass;

text:
LSTM
• Shortcomings of RNNs: distant information
• Distant information is critical to many language applications.
• To train RNNs, it is difficult to make use of information distant from the current point of
processing.
– Alhough RNNs access to the entire preceding sequence, the information encoded in
hidden states tends to be fairly local, more relevant to the most recent parts of the
input.
Example: The flights the airline was canceling were full.
• Assigning a high probability to was following airline is straightforward since airline
provides a strong local context for the singular agreement.
• Assigning an appropriate probability to were is quite difficult because
• the plural flights is quite distant,
• the singular noun airline is closer in the intervening context.
• Ideally, a network should be able to retain the distant information about plural flights
until it is needed, while still processing the intermediate parts of the sequence correctly.
• LSTMs are capable of learning and remembering long-term dependencies between
time steps in a sequence  they are particularly effective for tasks like speech
recognition, language modeling, and time-series forecasting
29

1. The weights in the hidden layer are being asked to perform two tasks
simultaneously:
– provide information useful for the current decision, and
– updating and carrying forward information required for future decisions.
2. Training RNNs needs to backpropagate the error signal back through time.
– The hidden layer at time t contributes to the loss at the next time step since
it takes part in that calculation.
– During the backward pass of training, the hidden layers are
subject to repeated multiplications, as determined by the length of
the sequence.
– A frequent result of this process: the gradients are eventually driven to zero,
a situation called the vanishing gradients problem.
• More complex network architectures are designed to explicitly manage the
task of maintaining relevant context over time,
– by enabling the network to learn to forget information that is no longer
needed and
– to remember information required for decisions still to come.
 LSTM 30

text:
• The long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, extensions of
RNNs, are designed to solve context management problem.
• LSTMs divide the context management problem into two
subproblems:
– removing information no longer needed from the context, and
– adding information likely to be needed for later decision making.
• LSTMs accomplish the context management problem
Adding an explicit context layer to the architecture (in addition to the hidden
layer), and
Using specialized neural units that make use of gates to control the flow of
information into and out of the units that comprise the network layers.
These gates are implemented through the use of additional weights that
operate sequentially on the input, and previous hidden layer, and previous
context layers.

text:
LSTM
The gates in an LSTM share a common design pattern:
• Each consists of
• a feedforward layer,
• followed by a sigmoid activation function,
• followed by a pointwise multiplication with the layer being
gated.
• The sigmoid activation function is preferred because it pushes its
outputs to 0 or 1.
• A pointwise multiplication of the sigmoid function output and the
layer being gated has an effect similar to that of a binary mask of the
layer.
• Values in the layer being gated that align with values near 1 in the
mask are passed through nearly unchanged; values corresponding to
lower values are essentially erased.

Encoder-Decoder Model with RNNs
Four architectures for NLP tasks
In encoder-decoder model we have two
separate RNN models,
• First one maps input sequence to intermediate
representation, called a context; and
• Second one maps from context to output
sequence.
In sequence labeling (POS
tagging) we map each input
token xi to an output token yi.
In sequence classification
we map the entire input
sequence to a single class.
In language modeling we
output next token conditioned

text:
• The encoder-decoder model (sometimes called sequence-to-
sequence model) takes an input sequence and translates it to an
output sequence that is of a different length than the input.
• Encoder-decoder models: have been applied to a wide range of
applications including summarization, question answering, and
dialogue, but are particularly popular for machine translation
– input and output sequences can have different lengths and
– mapping between a token in the input and a token in the output
can be very indirect.
• Key idea: use of an encoder network that takes an input sequence
and creates a contextualized representation of it, often called the
context.
– This context representation is then passed to a decoder which
generates a task-specific output sequence.

text:
Encoder-Decoder Model with RNNs
The encoder-decoder architecture
Encoder-decoder networks consist of three conceptual components:
1. An encoder that accepts an input sequence, x1:n, and generates a corresponding
sequence of contextualized representations, h1:n.
• LSTMs and transformers can all be employed as encoders.
2. A context vector c, which is a function of h1:n, and conveys the essence of
the input to the decoder.
3. A decoder, which accepts c as input and generates an arbitrary length
sequence of hidden states h1:m, from which a corresponding sequence of
output states y1:m, can be obtained.
• Just as with encoders, decoders can be realized by any kind of
sequence architecture (RNNs, LSTMs, transformers).
42

text:
Training the Encoder-Decoder Model
• Encoder-decoder architectures are trained end-to-end.
• Each training example is a tuple of paired strings, a source and
a target.
• Concatenated with a separator token, these source-target pairs
can now serve as training data.
• For MT, the training data typically consists of sets of sentences
and their translations drawn from standard datasets of aligned
sentence pairs.
• The network is given the source text and then starting with the
separator token is trained autoregressively to predict the next
word.

text:
The Transformer
• It is the standard architecture for building large language
models.
• Transformer-based large language models have completely
changed the field of speech and language processing.
• We will focus for now on left-to-right (sometimes called
causal or autoregressive) language modeling.
• The transformer is a neural network with a specific
structure that includes a mechanism called self-attention or
multi-head attention.
• Attention : a way to build contextual representations of a
token’s meaning by attending to and integrating information
from surrounding tokens, helping the model learn how
tokens relate to each other over large spans.

text:
The Transformer
• A transformer has 3 major components:
 At the center are columns of transformer blocks.
 Each block is a multilayer network
 a multi-head attention layer,
 feedforward network and
 layer normalization
that maps an input vector xi in column i (corresponding
to input token i) to an output vector hi.
 The set of n blocks maps an entire context window of
input vectors (x1, …, xn) to a window of output vectors
(h1, …, hn) of the same length.
 A column might contain from 12 to 96 or more stacked
blocks.
8

text:
The Transformer
• The column of blocks is preceded by the input encoding
component, which processes an input token into a
contextual vector representation, using
 an embedding matrix E and
 a mechanism for encoding token position.
• Each column is followed by a language modeling head,
which
 takes the embedding output by the final transformer
block,
 passes it through an unembedding matrix U and
 a softmax over the vocabulary
to generate a single token for that column.

text:
Intuition of Attention
• These examples showcase that the contextual words that help us
compute the meaning of words in context can be quite far away in the
sentence or paragraph.
• Transformers can build contextual representations of word meaning,
contextual embeddings, by integrating the meaning of these helpful
contextual words.
• In a transformer, layer by layer, we build up richer and richer
contextualized representations of the meanings of input tokens.
• At each layer, we compute the representation of a token i by combining
information about i from the previous layer with information about the
neighboring tokens to produce a contextualized representation for each
word at each position.
• Intuition of Attention: Build up the contextual embedding from a
word by selectively integrating information from all the neighboring
words.
• We say that a word "attends to" some neighboring words more than
others. 15

text:
Learning the weight matrices WQ, WK, WV
• WQ, WK, and WV are learned during the training process via
backpropagation, just like any other learnable parameter in a
neural network.
• Preliminary key points:
 Transformers (and their attention mechanisms) are trained using
supervised learning
 A loss function (such as cross-entropy loss) is optimised by
adjusting the parameters of the network (including WQ, WK, and
WV).
 The goal of the attention mechanism is to compute a weighted sum
of the values, where the weights are determined by the attention
scores (computed from the queries and keys).
 Backpropagation is used to adjust the weights of WQ, WK, and
WV, based on the gradients computed from the loss function.

text:
Learning the weight matrices WQ, WK, WV
1. The Setup:
 At each position in a sequence, we have an embedding vector
for each token (e.g., ei for token i).
 The attention mechanism transforms these embeddings into
Query, Key, and Value vectors for each token, using the
weight matrices WQ, WK, and WV.
2. How the Attention Mechanism Works: The input embeddings
for a sequence (say, e1,e2,...,en​) are transformed into Query,
Key, and Value vectors as follows:
 Query (Q):    Qi=WQ⋅ei
where Qi ​ is the query vector for token i, and WQ is a learnable
weight matrix that transforms the embedding ei ​ into the Query
vector.
27

text:
Learning the weight matrices $W^Q$, $W^K$, $W^V$

3. Attention Calculation: For each Query $Q_i$, we compute the attention scores by measuring the similarity between $Q_i$ and the Keys of all tokens (including its own).
- This is done using the dot product scaled by the square root of the dimension of the key vectors $d_k$:
$$\text{Attention Score}(i, j) = \frac{Q_i \cdot K_j}{\sqrt{d_k}}$$
where $d_k$ is the dimension of the Key vector.

- These scores are then passed through a softmax function giving:
$$\text{Attention Weights}(i, j) = \text{softmax}\left( \frac{Q_i \cdot K_j}{\sqrt{d_k}} \right)$$

- Finally, the Value vectors are weighted by these attention scores to compute the output vector for Query $Q_i$:
$$\text{Output}_i = \sum_{j} \text{Attention Weights}(i, j) \cdot V_j$$

29

- This is done using the dot product scaled by the square root of the dimension of the key vectors $d_k$:

text:
4. Training and Backpropagation:
 The goal during training is to minimize a loss function (such as cross-entropy
loss in the case of language modeling or classification).
 Backpropagation is used to compute the gradients of the loss with respect to
the model parameters (including WQ, WK, and WV).
 Gradients: The gradients indicate how to adjust WQ, WK, and WV to reduce
the loss.
• For example, consider the loss with respect to the Query weight matrix
WQ: 𝛛𝐋𝛛𝑾𝑸
• This gradient tells the model how to adjust WQ based on the error between
the predicted output and the target.
 The gradients are then used to update the weights using an optimization
algorithm (typically stochastic gradient descent or one of its variants, such
as Adam). The updates are as : 𝑊𝑄 = 𝑊𝑄 − 𝜂 𝛛𝐋𝛛𝑾𝑸 (η: learning rate)
• The same process happens for WK and WV, with their respective gradients
being computed and used to update them. 30

text:
Why multi-head attention?
Different purposes: Each attention head might learn to attend
to different types of contextual relationships or dependencies
between tokens. E.g.:
• One attention head might focus on local dependencies,
paying attention to nearby words or tokens.
• Another head might focus on long-range dependencies,
capturing relationships between tokens that are far apart in
the sequence.
• A third head could focus on syntax or semantics, attending
to grammatical or meaning-related patterns in the text.
• Another head might capture word alignment across
different phrases or languages in tasks like translation.
33

The residual stream

transformer block is considered as a single stream of d-

38
• Here, the processing of an individual token i through the

text:
The residual stream
• The initial vector for token i is passed through a layer
norm and attention layer, and
• The result is added back into the stream, in this case
to the original input vector xi.
• This summed vector is again passed through another
layer norm and a feedforward layer,
• The output of those is added back into the residual,
• This result, referred to as hi, is the output of the
transformer block for token i.
• In earlier descriptions the residual stream was often
described as residual connections.
39

text:
Position Embeddings
• There are many methods, but we'll just describe the
simplest: absolute position.
• Goal: learn a position embedding matrix Epos of shape
[1 × N ].
• Start with randomly initialized embeddings, one for each
integer up to some maximum length.
(i.e., just as we have an embedding for token fish, we’ll have
an embedding for position 3 and position 17).
• As with word embeddings, these position embeddings are
learned along with other parameters during training.
60
• To produce an input embedding that captures positional
information, add the word embedding for each input to its
corresponding positional embedding.

text:
Alternatives to Position Embeddings
• Potential problem with the simple absolute position embedding
approach:
 there will be plenty of training examples for the initial positions in
our inputs and
 correspondingly fewer at the outer length limits.
  These latter embeddings may be poorly trained and may not
generalize well during testing.
• Alternative approach to absolute positional embeddings:
 Choose a static function that maps integer inputs to real-valued
vectors in a way that captures the inherent relationships among the
positions.
 That is, it captures the fact that position 4 in an input is more closely
related to position 5 than it is to position 17.
 A combination of sine and cosine functions with differing
frequencies was used in the original transformer work.
• Even more complex positional embedding methods exist, such as ones
that represent relative position instead of absolute position. 62

text:
Learning of the Multiple Heads
• After all heads compute their attention results,
these are concatenated and passed through a
linear transformation to produce the final
output.
• The concatenation of the different outputs from
all the heads allows the model to use the diverse
features that each head has learned.
•  even if each head individually doesn't
produce the same result, the final output
benefits from the combination of the distinct
insights provided by each head. 68

text:
Missed point
• How is dk determined?
• In the context of the scaled dot-product attention used in
Transformers, dk is a hyperparameter chosen before
training and is typically fixed.
• Usually chosen to be a smaller value than d, the input
embedding dimension.
 For example, if the embedding size d is 512, a common
choice for dk might be 64 or 128.
• The value of dk controls how much attention each token
can "focus on" relative to other tokens in the sequence.
• dk also affects the complexity of the attention mechanism,
as larger values of dk result in larger matrices and more
computation during attention.
69

text:
LLMs
• In this chapter we formalize the idea of pretraining:
learning knowledge about language and the world from
vast amounts of text—and call the resulting pretrained
language models Large Language Models (LLMs).
• LLMs have been transformative, especially in tasks
where text generation is required (MT, summarization,
QAS, chatbots...)
• Text generation, code generation, and image generation
together constitute the important new area of
generative AI.
• Almost any NLP task can be modeled as word
prediction in a large language model,

text:
Language models
• Remember the simple n-gram language model
• Assigns probabilities to sequences of words
• Generates text by sampling possible next words
• Is trained on counts computed from lots of text
• Large language models are similar and
different:
• Assign probabilities to sequences of words
• Generate text by sampling possible next words
• Are trained by learning to guess the next word
4

text:
Text Completion
• Example: simple task of text completion of “So long
and thanks for”
• Here a LM is given a text prefix and is asked to
generate a possible completion.
• During generation, the model has direct access to the
priming context as well as to all of its own
subsequently generated outputs (as fits in the large
context window).
• Key to the Power of LLMs built from transformers:
this ability to incorporate
 the entirety of the earlier context and
 generated outputs at each time step.

text:
LLMs for summarization (using  tl;dr)
• Give a LLM a text, and follow it by a token like tl;dr;
• Token tl;dr; is short for “too long; didn’t read” often
used, especially in informal work emails, when they are
going to give a short summary.
• This token being sufficiently frequent in LM training
data, the LM has seen many texts in which the token
occurs before a summary, and hence will interpret it as
instructions to generate a summary.
• So conditional generation  give the LM the prefix, and
then have it generate the following words, one by one.
• Take the entire response as a summary.
13

text:
Greedy Decoding
• One simple way to generate words is to always generate the
most likely word given the context.
• This is called greedy decoding (GD).
• A greedy algorithm is one that makes a locally optimal choice.
ෝ𝑤𝑡 = 𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑚𝑎𝑥𝑤∈𝑉𝑃(𝑤|𝑤<𝑡)
• In practice, greedy decoding not used with LLMs.
• Major problem with GD: because the words it chooses are
extremely predictable, the resulting text is generic and often
quite repetitive.
• GD will always result in generating exactly the same string.
• Beam Search, extension to GD, works well in tasks like MT.
• Most other tasks, more sophisticated methods, called sampling
methods, introduce more diversity into the generations.

text:
Decoding and Sampling
• Core of generation process for LLMs: task of choosing
the word to generate next based on the context and the
probabilities that the model assigns to possible words.
• This task is called decoding.
• Sampling: the most common method for decoding in
LLMs.
• Sampling from a model’s distribution over words:
choose random words according to their probability
assigned by the transformer model.
• After each token, sample words to generate according
to their probability conditioned on previous choices.

Random sampling Shortcoming

high-probable words,
- Problem: There are many odd, low-probability
words in the tail of the distribution

distribution.

text:
Top-k sampling:
• Top-k sampling is a simple generalization of greedy
decoding.
1. Choose # of words k
2. For each word in the vocabulary V , use the LM to
compute the likelihood of this word given the context
p(wt |w<t )
3. Sort the words by likelihood and keep only the top k
most probable words.
4. Renormalize the scores of the k words to be a
legitimate probability distribution.
5. Randomly sample a word from within these remaining
k most-probable words according to its probability.

text:
Temperature sampling
• Reshape the distribution instead of truncating it.
•Intuition from thermodynamics,
• a system at high temperature is flexible and can
explore many possible states;
• a system at lower temperature is likely to explore
a subset of lower energy (better) states.
• In low-temperature sampling,  (τ ≤ 1) we smoothly
• increase the probability of the most probable
words
• decrease the probability of the rare words.

text:
Temperature sampling
Why does this work?
• When τ is close to 1 the distribution doesn’t change
much.
• The lower τ is, the larger the scores being passed to the
softmax function.
• Softmax pushes high values toward 1 and low values
toward 0.
• Large input pushes high-probability words higher and
low probability word lower,  making the distribution
more greedy.
• As τ approaches 0, the probability of most likely word
approaches 1 .
0 ≤ τ ≤ 1

text:
Self-supervised training algorithm
• Model just trained to predict the next word!
1. Take a corpus of text
2. At each time step t
i. ask the model to predict the next word ;
ii. train the model using gradient descent to minimize
the error in this prediction.
• Model called self-supervised because no need to add
any special gold labels to the data; the natural sequence
of words is its own supervision!
• Model trained to minimize the error in predicting the
true next word in the training sequence, using cross-
entropy as the loss function. 30

text:
Teacher forcing
• At each token position t, model sees correct tokens w1:t,
• Computes  loss (–log probability) for the next token wt+1
• At next token position t+1 we ignore what the  model
predicted for wt+1
• Instead we take the correct word wt+1, add it to context,
move on.
• For training, the probability assigned to the correct word is
used to calculate the CE loss for each item in the sequence.
• The loss for a training sequence is the average cross-entropy
loss over the entire sequence.
• Weights in the network are adjusted to minimize the average
CE loss over the training sequence via gradient descent.
33

text:
On LLM Training
• Large models are generally trained by filling
the full context window with text.
 For example, 4096 tokens for GPT4 or 8192 for
Llama 3.
• If documents are shorter than this, multiple
documents are packed into the window with a
special end-of-text token between them.
• The batch size for gradient descent is usually
quite large:
 the largest GPT-3 model uses a batch size of 3.2
million tokens.
34

text:
Parallelising & distributing the Computation
• Time-sharing is used so as multiple sequences are
processed simultaneously, with resources (like
GPUs/TPUs) taking turns processing different parts of
the batch in parallel.
• The parallelism exists both within sequences (intra-
sequence, e.g., attention heads) and across sequences
(inter-sequence, e.g., parallel batches of sequences
processed across GPUs/TPUs).
• Parallelism and distributed processing are what makes
training on such large datasets and models possible.
35

text:
Filtering for Quality and Safety
• Quality is subjective!
• Quality filters are classifiers that assign scores to each doc.
• Need to remove unwanted material such as Personal
Identifiable Information (PII) and adult content.
• Deduplication at many levels (URLs, documents, even
lines)
• Quality filtering usually improve LM performance.
• Safety is also subjective.
• Toxicity detection is important, although that has mixed
results.
• Can mistakenly flag data written in dialects like African
American English
• LMs trained on toxicity-filtered content fail to detect toxicity.

text:
Finetuning
• What happens if we need our LLM to work well
on a domain it didn't see in pretraining?
• Perhaps some specific medical or legal domain or
task?
• Or maybe a multilingual LM needs to see more
data on some language that was rare in
pretraining?
• We can simply continue training the model on
relevant data from the new domain or language.
• Finetuning: process of taking a fully pretrained
model and running additional training passes on
some new data. 42

text:
Perplexity
• The higher the probability of the word
sequence, the lower the perplexity.
• Thus the lower the perplexity of a model on
the data, the better the model.
• Minimizing perplexity is the same as
maximizing probability
• Also: perplexity is sensitive to length /
tokenization so best used when comparing
LMs that use the same tokenizer.
49

Scaling Laws
• LLM performance depends mainly on 3 factors:
1. Model size: the number of parameters not
counting embeddings
• Llama 3.1 405B Instruct model from Meta: 405 billion
parameters (126 layers, embedding dimension of 16,384,
128 attention heads) and trained on over 15 trillion tokens
using a vocabulary of 128K tokens.
• GPT-4o: estimated by many at 1.76 trillion parameters,
context window 128K tokens, max output 16,384
tokens.
• GPT-3: 175 billion parameters; embedding dimension of
12,288.

text:
Scaling Laws
2. Dataset size: the amount of training data
• Llama 3.1 405B trained on over 15 trillion tokens.
• GPT-4 trained on 13 trillion tokens.
3. Compute: amount of compute (e.g. in FLOPS):
typically in the order of exaflops during training
(1 exaflop = 1018 FLOPS).
• A model can be improved  by adding  parameters (more
layers, wider contexts), more data, or training for more
iterations.
• The performance of a large language model (the loss)
scales as a power-law with each of these three.

text:
Parameter-Efficient Finetuning
• Adapting to a new domain by continued pretraining
(finetuning) is a problem with huge LLMs.
• Enormous numbers of parameters to train
• Each pass of batch gradient descent has to backpropagate
through many many huge layers.
• Expensive in processing power, in memory, and in time.
• Instead, parameter-efficient fine tuning (PEFT)
• Efficiently select a subset of parameters to update when
finetuning. E.g.
• freeze some of the parameters (don’t change them),
• and only update some particular subset of parameters.
56

text:
LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation)
• Intuition: Transformers have many dense matrix
layers that are used in multiplications
• Like WQ, WK, WV, WO layers in attention
• Instead of updating these layers during finetuning,
• Freeze these layers
• Update a low-rank approximation with fewer
parameters.
• So LoRA provides an approach to adapting large
models while significantly reducing the computational
cost and memory footprint.
57

LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation)
• Intuition: Transformers have many dense matrix
layers that are used in multiplications
• Like WQ, WK, WV, WO layers in attention
• Instead of updating these layers during finetuning,
• Freeze these layers

• So LoRA provides an approach to adapting large

text:
LoRA
• Consider a matrix W (shape [d × dk])  that needs to be updated
during finetuning via gradient descent.
• Normally, after Gradient Descent, W gets updates ∆W  (of
shape [d × dk])
• In LoRA, W is frozen and, instead, a low-rank decomposition of
W is updated (through training):
• A of shape [d × r],
• B of shape [r × dk],    where r very small   (e.g. 1, 2, 4, 8, 16)
• So, during  finetuning, we update A and B instead of W.
• Replace W + ∆W with W + B A.
• In forward pass, instead of h = x W, we do   h = x W + x A B
• So LoRA introduces low-rank matrices that are trained, while the
original pre-trained weight matrices remain frozen.
58

text:
Bidirectional Transformer Encoders
• Bidirectional Transformer Encoders are pretrained
language models, trained via masked language
modeling.
• Instead of predicting the following word, we mask a
word in the middle and ask the model to guess the
word given the words on both sides.
• This method thus allows the model to see both the
right and left context.
• The most widely-used masked language modeling
architecture is BERT (Bidirectional Encoder
Representations from Transformers)

text:
Bidirectional Transformer Encoders
• Bidirectional Encoders (such as BERT) make use of Transformer, an
attention mechanism that learns contextual relations between words (or
sub-words) in a text.  contextualized representations
• Bidirectional encoders use self-attention to
map input embeddings (x1,…,xn) to output
embeddings (a1,…,an) the same length, where
the output vectors have been contextualized
using information from the entire input
sequence.
• Encoder that reads the text input and Decoder that produces a
prediction for the task.
• Since BERT’s goal is to generate a language model, only the encoder
mechanism is necessary.
– Bidirectional Encoders produce an encoding for each input token but
generally aren’t used to produce running text by decoding/sampling.
6

text:
• The original English-only bidirectional transformer encoder model
BERT consisted of:
– An English-only subword vocabulary consisting of 30,000 tokens.
– Hidden layers of size 768,
– 12 layers of transformer blocks, with 12 (bidirectional) multihead
attention layers each.
– The resulting model has about 100M parameters.
• The larger multilingual XLM-RoBERTamodel, trained on 100
languages, has:
– A multilingual subword vocabulary with 250,000 tokens.
– 24 layers of transformer blocks, with 16 multihead attention layers
each
– Hidden layers of size 1024
– Input context window of 512 tokens
– The resulting model has about 550M parameters.

text:
• A causal (backward looking) transformer language model
is trained by iteratively predicting the next word in a text.
– This approach does not work with bidirectional encoders
because the next word is given in the context.
• Biderectional transformer encoder language models are
trained by predicting the missing elements in a text.
– Given an input sequence with one or more elements
missing, the learning task is to predict the missing
elements.
– During training, the model must generate a probability
distribution over the vocabulary for each of the missing
items.

text:
Training Bidirectional Encoders
• The original approach to training bidirectional encoders is called
Masked Language Modeling (MLM).
• MLM uses unannotated text from a large corpus.
• The model is presented with a series of sentences from the
training corpus, where a random sample of tokens from each
training sequence is selected for use in the learning task.
• Once chosen, a token is used in one of three ways:
a. It is replaced with the unique vocabulary token [MASK];
b. It is replaced with another token from the vocabulary,
randomly sampled based on token unigram probabilities;
c. It is left unchanged.
• In BERT,15% of the input tokens in a training sequence are sampled
for learning. Of these,
o 80% are replaced with [MASK],
o 10% are replaced with randomly selected tokens, and
o the remaining 10% are left unchanged. 13

text:
Training Bidirectional Encoders
• The MLM training objective is to predict the original inputs for
each of the masked tokens using a bidirectional encoder.
• The cross-entropy loss from these predictions drives the training
process for all the parameters in the model.
• Note that all the input tokens play a role in the self-attention
process, but only the sampled tokens are used for learning.
Input:
• The original input sequence is first tokenized using a subword
model.
• The sampled items which drive the learning process are chosen
from among the set of tokenized inputs.
• Word embeddings for all the tokens in the input are retrieved from
the word embedding matrix and then combined with positional
embeddings to form the input to the transformer. 14

• In this example, long, thanks and the have been sampled from the training
sequence, with the first two masked and the replaced with the randomly

yi = softmax(WV zi)

text:
Training Bidirectional Encoders
• The focus of mask-based learning is on predicting words from
surrounding contexts with the goal of producing effective word-
level representations.
• An important class of applications involves determining the
relationship between pairs of sentences
– paraphrase detection (detecting if two sentences have similar
meanings)
– entailment (detecting if the meanings of two sentences entail or
contradict each other)
– discourse coherence (deciding if two neighboring sentences
form a coherent discourse)
• To capture the kind of knowledge required for applications such as
these, BERT introduced a second learning objective called Next
Sentence Prediction (NSP).
18

text:
Training Bidirectional Encoders
• In BERT,50% of the training pairs consisted of positive pairs, and
in the remaining 50% the 2nd sentence of a pair was randomly
selected from elsewhere in the corpus.
• The NSP loss is based on how well the model can distinguish true
pairs from random pairs.
• BERT introduces two new tokens to the input representation:
– After tokenizing the input with the subword model, the token
[CLS] is prepended to the input sentence pair, and the token
[SEP] is placed between the sentences and after the final token
of the second sentence.
– During training, the output vector from the final layer
associated with the [CLS] token represents the next sentence
prediction.

text:
Training Bidirectional Encoders
• The original BERT models were trained on about 3.3 billion words.
– Modern masked LMs are now trained on much larger datasets of web text
– The XLM-RoBERTamodel was trained on about 300 billion tokens in
100 languages.
• To train the original BERT models, pairs of text segments were selected from
the training corpus according to the next sentence prediction 50/50 scheme.
– Pairs were sampled with a combined length of less than the 512 token input.
– Tokens within these sentence pairs were then masked using the MLM
approach with the combined loss from the MLM and NSP objectives used for
a final loss.
• Some models, like the RoBERTamodel, drop the next sentence prediction
objective, and therefore change the training regime a bit.
– Instead of sampling pairs of sentences, the input is simply a series of
contiguous sentences.
– If the document runs out before 512 tokens are reached, an extra separator
token is added, and sentences from the next document are packed in, until we
reach a total of 512 tokens.
21

text:
• The power of pretrained LMs lies in their ability to extract generalizations
from huge amounts of text that are useful for many NLP applications.
• Fine-tuning: process of taking the network learned by pretrained models,
and further training the model, via an added neural net classifier that takes the
top layer of the network as input, to perform some task like sequence
classification or named entity tagging.
– The pretraining phase learns a LM that instantiates rich representations
of word meaning, that thus enables the model to more easily learn (‘be
fine-tuned to’) the requirements of a downstream language
understanding task.
– Pretrain-finetune paradigm is an instance of transfer learning in
machine learning: the method of knowledge learning in one task or
domain, and then applying it (transferring it) to solve a new task.
• The fine-tuning process consists of using labeled data about the
application to train these additional application-specific parameters.
– This training will either freeze or make only minimal adjustments to the
pretrained LM parameters.
Fine-Tuning Language Models

text:
Fine-Tuning Language Models
• Sequence classification applications often represent an input
sequence with a single consolidated representation.
• In transformer models, an additional vector is added to the
model to stand for the entire sentence sequence.
– This vector is called the sentence embedding since it refers to
the entire sequence.
– In BERT,the [CLS] token plays the role of this embedding.
– This unique token is added to the vocabulary and is
prepended to the start of all input sequences, both during
pretraining and encoding.
• The output vector in the final layer of the model for the [CLS]
input represents the entire input sequence and serves as the input
to a classifier head, a logistic regression or neural network
classifier that makes the relevant decision.

id: Chapter 14_Question Answering, Information Retrievak and RAG_p2
document: Chapter 14_Question Answering, Information Retrievak and RAG
text:
Question Answering Systems (QAS)
• QASs are designed to fill human information needs.
• Since a lot of information is in text form (web, books, emails,
etc.), QA is closely related to the task behind search engines.
• QASs often focus on factoid questions (What, Where, When,
etc.) that can be answered with simple facts expressed in short
or medium-length texts. E.g.:
• What time does the Bardo Museum open?
• Where does the energy in a nuclear
explosion come from?
• When did Algeria get its independence?

id: Chapter 14_Question Answering, Information Retrievak and RAG_p3
document: Chapter 14_Question Answering, Information Retrievak and RAG
text:
QASs using LLMs
• Modern NLP systems answer these questions using LLMs, in
one of two ways.
• The first is to prompt a pretrained LLM that has been
finetuned on question/answer datasets with the question in
the prompt.
E.g. causal language model with a string like:
Q: Where is the Louvre Museum located? A:
have it do conditional generation given this prefix, and take
the response as the answer.
• Idea: LMs have read a lot of facts in their pretraining data,
(presumably including the location of the Louvre), and
have encoded this information in their parameters.
3

id: Chapter 14_Question Answering, Information Retrievak and RAG_p4
document: Chapter 14_Question Answering, Information Retrievak and RAG
text:
Problems with prompting an LLM
• Simply prompting an LLM can be a useful approach to answer
many factoid questions. But it is not yet a complete solution for QA.
• Problems:
 LLMs often hallucinate.
 When asked questions, LLMs can make up answers that sound
reasonable.
 E.g.: Dahl et al. (2024) found that when asked questions about
the legal domain (e.g. particular legal cases), LLMs hallucinated
69% to 88% of the time!
• Not always possible to tell when LMs are hallucinating, partly
because LLMs aren’t well-calibrated.
• In a calibrated system, the confidence of a system in the
correctness of its answer is highly correlated with the probability of
an answer being correct  if a calibrated system is wrong, at least it
might hedge its answer or tell us to go check another source. 4

id: Chapter 14_Question Answering, Information Retrievak and RAG_p5
document: Chapter 14_Question Answering, Information Retrievak and RAG
text:
Problems with prompting an LLM
• Other problems:
 Simply prompting a LLM doesn’t allow one to ask questions
about proprietary data (e.g. personal emails, medical records,
internal company documents, …).
 Static LLMs have problems with questions about rapidly
changing information (e.g. about an event that happened last
week) since LLMs won’t have up-to-date information from
after their release data.
• For this reason the most common way to do question-answering
with LLMs is retrieval-augmented generation or RAG.
• In RAG information retrieval (IR) techniques are used to retrieve
documents likely to have information that might help answer the
question. Then a LLM is used to generate an answer given these
documents.
5

id: Chapter 14_Question Answering, Information Retrievak and RAG_p6
document: Chapter 14_Question Answering, Information Retrievak and RAG
text:
RAG for the LLM IR problems
• Basing the answers on retrieved documents can solve some of
the problems with using simple prompting to answer
questions.
 It helps ensure that the answer is grounded in facts from
some curated dataset.
 The system can give the user the answer accompanied by
the context of the passage or document the answer came
from  This information can help users have confidence in
the accuracy of the answer (or help them spot when it is
wrong!).
 These retrieval techniques can be used on any proprietary
data we want, such as legal or medical data for those
applications.
6

id: Chapter 14_Question Answering, Information Retrievak and RAG_p7
document: Chapter 14_Question Answering, Information Retrievak and RAG
text:
Information Retrieval (IR)
• Information Retrieval: the field encompassing the retrieval of
all forms of media based on user information needs.
• The resulting IR system is often called a search engine.
• We consider ad hoc retrieval where a user poses a query to a
retrieval system, which then returns an ordered set of documents
from some collection.
• A document: refers to any unit of text the system indexes and
retrieves (web pages, scientific papers, news articles, or even
shorter passages like collection paragraphs).
• A collection: refers to a set of documents being used to satisfy
user term requests.
• A term: refers to a word in a collection, but it may also include
phrases.
• A query: a user’s information need expressed as a set of terms.
7

id: Chapter 14_Question Answering, Information Retrievak and RAG_p8
document: Chapter 14_Question Answering, Information Retrievak and RAG
text:
High-level architecture of an ad-hoc
retrieval engine
• The basic IR architecture uses the vector space model.
• Queries and documents are mapped to vectors based on unigram word
counts.
• Cosine similarity between the vectors used to rank potential documents.
• This is an example of the bag-of-words model (ref. Chap. 4), since
words are considered independently of their positions.
8

Another term weighting scheme: BM25
• BM25 (Best Matching 25) ranks documents based on their
relevance to a given query.
• BM25 is an extension of the TF-IDF model, designed to improve
performance by incorporating the idea that term frequency should

relevance, BM25 introduces non-linear effects to better match
real-world information retrieval needs, especially when the TF
grows very high.
